newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Kremlin rattles election sword in Duma budget war.
newsitem.headline: Kremlin rattles election sword in Duma budget war.

text.p: The war of nerves between Russia's reformist government and opposition-dominated parliament over tax reform and the budget intensified on Tuesday as the Kremlin brandished the threat of elections if it does not get its way.

President Boris Yeltsin and acting government leader Anatoly Chubais both called on the State Duma (lower house) to pass a new tax code before its summer recess in three weeks. Ministers say the code is vital to end the crisis in the economy and in the state finances. Next year's budget is to be based on it.
"Boris Yeltsin considers that the Duma should pass the tax code on the first reading before the recess," Interfax news agency quoted a spokesman as saying after Yeltsin met Chubais.
Neither spelled out the election threat, rumours of which have grown in recent days as they have many times before.

But First Deputy Prime Minister Chubais gave an interview to the business newspaper Kommersant Daily headlined "Chubais Gives Duma Three Weeks". In a preface the paper said: "If the 1998 budget is not accepted, the president may dissolve the Duma."
Opposition legislators, including the communist speaker of the Duma, saw it as an empty threat that they have heard before.

Most said early elections would not return a more pliant chamber. Some noted that, as President Jacques Chirac has just found in France, dissolution is a double-edged sword, giving voters a chance to vent their anger at an unpopular executive.

"The authorities are very nervous. They're looking for someone to blame for their own mistakes," Duma speaker Gennady Seleznyov told reporters. "But they're analysing Chirac's experience and clearly don't want to repeat that mistake."
Chubais, asked by Kommersant about a dissolution, declined to be drawn explicitly, saying it was up to Yeltsin to decide.
Government spokesman Igor Shabdurasulov told reporters dissolving the Duma was "not on the agenda at the moment".

But Chubais, who is also finance minister, stressed the urgency of pushing through the tax code, aimed at easing an unfairly distributed and complex tax burden. He is also impatient with the Duma for simply postponing a debate last month on big 1997 spending cuts. It is now due on June 11.

"We cannot wait, the economy and the people cannot wait. That's why we are taking such a tough position," said Chubais, who will head the cabinet until Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin returns from holiday on June 20.
Seleznyov, however, seems in no mood to rush. "We're not the fire brigade," he said. If the tax code was not passed by the recess on June 21 it would have to wait, he said.
Rumours of dissolution surface periodically in a political system where the government commands no majority in parliament and relies on the president's vast power to push through policy.
"There's nothing to this rumour," said Alexei Mitrofanov, of Vladimir Zhirinovsky's nationalist Liberal Democrats. "It's just to put pressure on the Duma to make it more compliant."

The rumours have been part of a familiar minuet in the 18 months of the present parliament, in which communists and their allies are the biggest group. They can block legislation but do not have the two-thirds majority needed to oust Yeltsin and have chosen not to carry out threats to vote down the government.

A simple majority on two no-confidence motions three months apart would force Yeltsin to make a choice between a new cabinet or new elections, which are not due till December 1999. But the opposition, after their defeat in last July's presidential election, have preferred a war of attrition to win concessions.
Yet some analysts believe the phoney war may be heating up.
Communist sources said various groups in the party were now weighing up when best to try to vote down the government.

Some favour an autumn attack, prompting elections in the middle of a harsh Russian winter when voters are at their most unhappy. Other communists fear an early election could further split the divided opposition, granting Yeltsin a freer hand.

Moskovskiye Novosti weekly said on Tuesday that Kremlin aides were also looking at provoking a break with the Duma if it continued to stall the economic reforms which have speeded up since Chubais was brought into the government three months ago.
The paper noted that Yeltsin was impatient to push through reforms in his remaining three years in office and could use the months between dissolution and an election to rule by decree.

Moskovskiye Novosti said the Duma could still compromise with the Kremlin: "But if the deputies do not limit themselves to threatening declarations and refuse all the government's suggestions, then the political summer could be a hot one."
